🎧 > Many people think that being bilingual makes children confused. In fact, research suggests the opposite. In one study in Canada, bilingual children performed better on tasks that required switching attention. This is probably because they constantly choose between two languages, which trains the brain's control system. Of course, the study had a small sample, so we need more research. Still, the findings challenge the old belief.
“Of course, the study had a small sample”
Why does the professor mention the study in Canada?
To support the claim that bilingualism helps attention.

content.text: Today let's talk about why some species become invasive. An invasive species is one that is introduced to a new area and spreads quickly, causing harm.
A common assumption is that invasive species are simply stronger than native ones. But that's not really the full picture.
Take the cane toad in Australia. It was introduced in 1935 to control beetles in sugar cane fields. Instead, it spread across millions of square kilometers.
The reason it succeeded wasn't strength — it was the absence of predators. Australian animals had never seen this toad, so they didn't know it was poisonous, and many died after eating it.
In fact, a study of northern quolls, a small native predator, found that their populations fell by more than 90% in some regions after the toads arrived.
Now, admittedly, not every introduced species becomes a problem. Most of them actually fail to survive.
So the lesson for scientists is that the new environment matters as much as the species itself.
